Literature Review
The brain tumor’s accurate and on-time detection is important for effective treatment and recovery at an early
stage in the E-healthcare system. Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques particularly machine learning (ML) and
deep learning (DL)-based computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems play important roles in the detection of
critical diseases. The AI-based CAD system effectively interprets the MRI images of brain tumors as compared
to medical doctors. However, AI-based CAD system predictive accuracy of interpreting the images is still not
enough to accurately detect the brain tumor. To tackle the accurate detection problem of brain tumors various
researchers proposed different methods using machine learning deep learning techniques. In this research work,
we have explored various brain tumor detection methods to find the research gap in the domain and designed a
new method to accurately detect brain tumors using machine learning and deep learning techniques.
Haq et al.4 proposed a new automated diagnostic framework for accurate brain cancer diagnosis, utilizing
deep learning techniques in an intelligent integrated model (CNN-LSTM) on BTDS, MBNDS, and BMIDS
datasets. The proposed model achieved high accuracy as compared to baseline models. ­Methil5 introduces a
novel method using brain imaging to identify brain cancers, utilizing equalization of histograms and methods
for opening, followed by a convolutional neural network for classification, achieving high accuracy. In another
study, Jia and ­Chen6 proposed a novel approach called fully automatic heterogeneous segmentation using sup-
port vector machines (FAHS-SVM) for accurately segmenting brain tumors using deep learning techniques in
MRI scans. Manogaran et al.7 use a machine learning technique for analyzing orthogonal gamma distributions
for brain tumors, identifying abnormalities through the identification of regions of interest. Polly et al.8 work
presents a computerized system using a support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish between healthy brain
MRI images and abnormal brain tumors, achieving high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.
Raut et al.9 proposed a CNN model for brain tumor detection, trained using pre-processed MRI scans, achiev-
ing 95.55% accuracy. K-means clustering is applied to identify specific tumor regions.

• Decision Trees (DT): Decision Trees are a common machine learning model for classification, regression, and medical
image analysis. They function by recursively partitioning data based on feature values, creating a tree-like structure
for decision- making [18]. In brain tumor detection, DTs classify tumor types by identifying hierarchical patterns in MRI
features. Their simplicity and interpretability make them well-suited for medical applications, and when integrated
with ensemble methods like Random Forests, they achieve greater accuracy and robustness [19].
• Random Forest (RF): Random Forest is an ensemble learning method that enhances classification and regression
accuracy by combining multiple decision trees [19]. It operates by aggregating predictions from several trees, reducing
overfitting and improving generalization. In brain tumor detection, RF effectively analyzes MRI features to distinguish
between tumor types with high accuracy and robust- ness. Its ability to handle high-dimensional data and resist noise
makes it a reliable choice for medical image classification and segmentation.
• K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN): K-Nearest Neighbours is a basic yet efficient machine learning technique used for
categorisation applications, such as medical picture analysis. It classifies data points based on the majority class of
their nearest neighbors in feature space [20]. In brain tumor detection, KNN identifies tumor types by comparing MRI
features to those of known cases. Its non-parametric nature allows it to adapt to complex patterns, making it a useful
tool for tumor classification, especially when combined with feature selection techniques to enhance accuracy and
efficiency.

Related Work
The realm of medical imaging, especially in the diagnosis
and classification of brain tumors using MRI scans, has
been a subject of extensive research, leading to significant
advancements over the years. This section delves into the
related work, focusing on traditional methods, the advent
of machine learning techniques, and the groundbreaking
shift towards deep learning approaches.
Traditional methods in brain tumor analysis
Initially, brain tumor detection and classification in MRI
scans relied heavily on manual interpretation by radiolo­
gists. This process involved scrutinizing MRI scans to
identify irregularities indicative of tumors. While effec­
tive to a degree, this approach was fraught with chal­
lenges such as high variability in tumor appearance and
the potential for human error, leading to inconsistent
diagnosis accuracy.
Early machine learning techniques
To mitigate these challenges, early machine learning
techniques were introduced. These methods typically
involved feature extraction from MRI images, where
characteristics like shape, texture, and intensity were
used to identify tumors. Classic algorithms like Sup­
port Vector Machines (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors
(k-NN), and decision trees were employed for classifica­
tion. Though these techniques improved the objectivity
in diagnosis, they were limited by the need for manual
feature selection and their inability to process the high-
dimensional data inherent in MRI images effectively.
Emergence of deep learning
The emergence of deep learning, particularly CNNs,
marked a significant shift in medical image analysis.
Unlike traditional machine learning, CNNs have the abil­
ity to automatically learn complex patterns directly from
the data, eliminating the need for manual feature extrac­
tion. This capability made them particularly suitable for
high-dimensional data like MRI scans.
Recent advances
Recent research has focused on addressing these chal­
lenges. For example, techniques like data augmentation
have been used to effectively increase the size of train­
ing datasets. Furthermore, advances in explainable AI,
such as Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
(Grad-CAM), have been employed to provide visual
explanations of CNN decisions, thereby enhancing the
interpretability of these models [9].

2 provided that the Rotation Invariant Vision Transformer (RViT) deep learning algorithm
classifies brain tumors from MRI data. Rotated patch embeddings increase tumor detection. The model
outperforms the Vision Transformer model and other methods in medical imaging. RViT’s specific design and
rotational invariance technique should improve brain tumor detection and other challenging imaging tasks.
Talaat et al.23 presented an AI-based Brain Tumour Detection (BTD) model, which diagnoses brain tumours
using MRI more efficiently and accurately than traditional approaches. An Image Processing Module (IPM) uses
Improved Grey Wolf Optimisation (IGWO) to extract and select features from MRI data, a Patient Detection
Module (PDM) uses classifiers to diagnose, and Explainable AI (XAI) improves decision-making transparency.
The BTD model has 98.8% accuracy, 97% precision, 97.5% recall, and 97.2% F-measure on 98 normal and 154
abnormal cases, suggesting it could enhance brain tumour diagnosis and therapy.
Gopu et al.24 highlighted that medical imaging is essential for brain tumour diagnosis, but deep learning
algorithms suffer from overfitting and excessive computing costs. Segmentation, feature extraction, and
classification are integrated in the lightweight quantum dilated attention convolutional neural network LMAQDAC.
Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping pinpoints tumour locations and increases interpretability, while
the improved Hiking optimisation technique speeds up and stabilises training. Compression allows real-time
performance on compact devices with 99.96% accuracy, 99.4% F1-score, and 94.8% Dice coefficient, providing
an enhanced framework for clinical brain tumour classification and segmentation.
This study proposed a novel deep learning-based model for automatic brain tumor classification using MRI
images by embedding a sophisticated convolutional network with optimized feature learning25. The proposed
approach increased the classification accuracy by implementing effective feature extraction and preprocessing
techniques on spatial data. Experimental results showed competitive accuracy with enhanced generalization
performance, indicating the increasing significance of hybrid deep learning systems for accurate and explainable
medical image analysis.
